summary.text: A knight is a person given the honorary title of knighthood by a head of state or a representative, for service to the monarch, the church or the country, especially in a military capacity.
In the Early Middle Ages knighthood was conferred upon mounted warriors, and often a knight was a vassal who served as an elite fighter or bodyguard for a lord, paid with land.
By the Late Middle Ages the rank was tied to chivalry, a code of conduct for the perfect courtly Christian warrior.

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Old English cniht, meaning boy or servant

facts.label: First knights
facts.value: Appeared during Charlemagne's reign in the 8th century

facts.label: Ceremony roots
facts.value: Grew from the older Carolingian presenting of weapons

paragraphs.heading: A title for service
paragraphs.text: A knight is someone given the honorary title of knighthood by a head of state, the pope included, or by their representative, to reward service to a monarch, church or country, especially military service. What that meant changed across the Middle Ages. Early on, knighthood went to warriors on horseback. In the High Middle Ages knights counted as a class of lesser nobility, and by the late Middle Ages the rank was bound up with chivalry, a code of behaviour for the ideal courtly Christian warrior.

paragraphs.heading: Knight and lord
paragraphs.text: A knight was often a vassal who served a lord as an elite fighter or bodyguard and was paid in land. Lords trusted their knights, who were skilled at fighting from the saddle. From the 12th century until the 15th, when it became a fashion among the high nobility of the Duchy of Burgundy, knighthood was closely tied to riding, and above all to the joust. You can still hear that link in words like chivalry, cavalier and the French title chevalier.

paragraphs.heading: From boy to warrior
paragraphs.text: The English word comes from Old English cniht, meaning 'boy' or 'servant', a cousin of German Knecht. Its sense drifted from 'boy' to 'household retainer', and by 1100 it had narrowed to a military follower of a king or other superior. The specific military sense, a horseman in the heavy cavalry, emerges only with the Hundred Years' War. The verb 'to knight' arrived around 1300, when 'knighthood' also stopped meaning 'adolescence' and came to mean a knight's rank.

paragraphs.heading: Words for riders
paragraphs.text: Medieval Latin called a knight miles, a word that in classical Latin meant a soldier, normally one on foot. In the later Roman Empire, everyday speech replaced equus, the classical word for horse, with caballus. From caballus came Italian cavaliere, Spanish caballero and French chevalier, the source of chivalry. Germanic languages took another path: German Ritter and Dutch and Scandinavian ridder come from rīdan, 'to ride'.

paragraphs.heading: The first knights
paragraphs.text: The Franks mostly fielded large infantry armies, with an elite that rode to battle on horseback. When Charles Martel's Frankish forces beat the Umayyad invasion at Tours in 732, they were still largely foot soldiers, with the elite dismounting to fight. The first knights appeared under Charlemagne in the 8th century, when any well-equipped horseman could be called a knight. As the Franks went on the attack in wide campaigns of conquest, more warriors rode with the emperor, and with the stirrup they more and more stayed in the saddle to fight as true cavalry.

paragraphs.heading: Dubbing and decline
paragraphs.text: Knighting ceremonies grew out of an older Carolingian custom of presenting a young man with weapons. A noble would be ritually handed arms and declared a knight, usually amid festivities. In the late Middle Ages new weapons such as the culverin, a gunpowder weapon aimed at people, began to make armoured knights obsolete, though the titles survived in many countries. Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I (1459–1519) is often called the 'last knight' for this reason.

paragraphs.heading: Stories and modern orders
paragraphs.text: Medieval literature spread the ideals of chivalry, above all through the Matter of France, about Charlemagne's paladins, and the Matter of Britain, about King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table. Today's orders of knighthood centre on charity and civic service rather than war. A head of state, monarch or senior churchman grants knighthood to recognise merit, often service to church or country. In English the female equivalent is a dame.
